contracts.name: Comp

health.headline: Nothing critical, and 3 medium severity issues worth a look.

contracts.purpose: Comp is the fixed-supply ERC-20 governance token of Compound. On top of standard balances and allowances, it lets holders delegate their voting power, directly or by EIP-712 signature. It records per-delegate vote checkpoints by block so historical voting power can be queried.

threats.title: Flash-borrowed voting power via same-block transfer and delegate
threats.target: Invariant: votes equal the sum of balances of delegators; getPriorVotes / checkpoints
threats.approach: An attacker borrows or flash-loans COMP, delegates to themselves (or receives it already delegated), and uses the votes in the same block. Voting power is only snapshotted per block, so a governance contract that reads getCurrentVotes, or a getPriorVotes call on a block where the attacker already moved tokens, can be swayed. The attacker then returns the tokens in the same block. The defense relies entirely on consumers using strictly prior blocks.

threats.title: Same-block checkpoint overwrite corrupts historical votes
threats.target: Invariant: at most one checkpoint per block, later change overwrites last checkpoint
threats.approach: An attacker makes several transfers or delegations in one block so _writeCheckpoint overwrites the last entry. If the overwrite or the numCheckpoints logic is wrong (e.g., the fromBlock comparison), the attacker could leave a stale or inflated votes value, or skip creating a new entry. A proposal snapshot taken at that block would then read incorrect voting power.

threats.title: Binary search in getPriorVotes returns wrong checkpoint
threats.target: Invariant: checkpoints ordered by strictly increasing fromBlock; getPriorVotes returns 0 if none at or before
threats.approach: An attacker builds a checkpoint history with boundary cases (a single checkpoint, a checkpoint exactly at the queried block, a query before the first checkpoint, or many checkpoints in consecutive blocks). The goal is to trigger an off-by-one in the binary search so that getPriorVotes reports higher votes than the account had at that block. This could inflate a proposal threshold or vote count.

threats.title: Votes attributed to or lost via the zero address
threats.target: Invariant: votes are never attributed to address(0); undelegated balances count for no one
threats.approach: A holder delegates to address(0), or a transfer occurs between accounts with delegate 0. If _moveDelegates does not skip the zero address, votes are minted to or burned from the zero checkpoint, or an underflow occurs on subtraction. A holder who re-delegates from 0 to a real delegate could then create votes out of nothing, or the call could revert and lock them out of transfers.

threats.title: Vote accounting drift between balances and delegate checkpoints
threats.target: Invariant: each account's votes equal the sum of balances of its delegators
threats.approach: An attacker finds a path where balances change without a matching _moveDelegates call. Candidates: self-transfer, a transfer of zero, transferFrom by the owner, or delegate called when source and destination delegates are equal. Votes would permanently diverge from balances, so a delegate accumulates more votes than the tokens delegated to it, or becomes unable to move votes out because of underflow reverts.

threats.title: delegateBySig signature replay or malleability
threats.target: Asset: nonces; Invariant: signature valid only for current nonce, before expiry, non-zero signer
threats.approach: A relayer or attacker replays a captured signature on another chain with the same contract address, replays after a fork, or submits a malleable (high-s) variant of the signature. If the domain separator omits the chain ID or contract address, or the signer is address(0) from an invalid signature, the attacker could change a victim's delegation or bump their nonce. They could also front-run to invalidate the victim's pending signed message (griefing).

threats.title: Allowance race and infinite-allowance handling
threats.target: Asset: allowances; Invariant: transferFrom decrements unless caller is source or allowance is uint96 max
threats.approach: A spender front-runs an owner's allowance change from N to M by spending N and then also spending M. An approve of uint256 max is truncated to uint96 max and never decremented, giving the spender unlimited access forever. Approving an amount of 2^96 or more that is not max reverts, so a miscalculated approval could be rejected or mis-stored.

threats.title: uint96 truncation or overflow in balances and votes
threats.target: Invariant: amounts of 2^96 or more are rejected; destination overflow reverts
threats.approach: An attacker passes crafted uint256 amounts to transfer, transferFrom or approve so that a downcast truncates silently. A truncated amount would debit less than credited or approve less or more than intended. Alternatively, vote sums exceeding uint96 in a delegate's checkpoint could revert and block transfers from delegators to that delegate.

threats.title: Delegate-targeted denial of service via checkpoint writes
threats.target: Asset: checkpoints / numCheckpoints; Invariant: block number fits in 32 bits
threats.approach: Many accounts delegate to a victim delegate and transfer dust amounts in many blocks. The attacker bloats the victim's checkpoint array, making getPriorVotes binary searches costlier. Any arithmetic revert in the checkpoint write path (block number cast, numCheckpoints increment, vote subtraction underflow) blocks all transfers for accounts delegating to that victim.

threats.title: Wrong constructor recipient locks or concentrates supply
threats.target: Asset: balances; Invariant: constant total supply minted to constructor account
threats.approach: The deployer passes address(0), an uncontrolled address or a wrong address as `account`. The entire 10M supply is then burned or locked with no mint or admin recovery, or concentrated in one key. The initial balance also starts undelegated, so those tokens count for no votes until the holder calls delegate.

findings.title: Floating Pragma
findings.description: Using ^ allows compilation with future compiler versions that may have bugs
findings.fix: Lock pragma to a specific version for production contracts

findings.title: Block Timestamp Dependency
findings.description: Block timestamps can be manipulated by miners within a short range
findings.fix: Avoid using timestamps for critical logic or accept ~15 second variance
Key the state by the caller where the value is theirs, or split a shared counter into stripes that sum back.
findings.title: 6 storage slots serialise this contract
findings.description: Every write to these forces the entrypoints touching them into a queue on Monad: balances, checkpoints, delegates, numCheckpoints, allowances, nonces.

findings.fix: Bound the loops, or let callers process a range they choose so the work per transaction is theirs to cap.
findings.title: 10 functions have no gas bound
findings.description: solc could not bound these, so their cost depends on a loop whose length is decided at runtime and a caller can push them past the block gas limit: allowance, approve, delegate, delegateBySig, getCurrentVotes, getPriorVotes, name, symbol, transfer, transferFrom.

findings.fix: Bound the loops, and have your frontend set an explicit gas limit for operations whose cost is fixed rather than letting the wallet estimate and pad.
findings.title: Gas variance costs real money on Monad
findings.description: Monad debits the sender for the transaction's gas limit, not the gas it uses, so anything a wallet pads onto the estimate is spent. solc cannot bound allowance(address,address), approve(address,uint256), delegate(address) and 7 more, which is where wallets fall back to a large default limit. Affects monad. Unbounded functions: 10.

findings.fix: Group state that is read together into a struct so it lands on one page. Each mapping key gets its own page, but a struct stored under that key shares it.
findings.title: Storage is spread too thinly to amortise Monad's page charge
findings.description: 4 slots across 4 pages. Monad pays 8,100 gas for the first touch of each 128-slot page, so slots that sit alone on a page cost more than they would on a per-slot schedule. Summed over the 3 calls traced, that is +23,700 gas. Affects monad. Storage delta: +23,700 gas.

findings.title: Contract is shaped for parallel execution
findings.description: 5 of 5 entrypoints can run concurrently, grade B. 0 of 15 entrypoint pairs always collide, and 11 more collide when they touch the same key, on balances, checkpoints, delegates. This only converts into throughput on a chain that executes transactions in parallel. Monad does; every other chain in this comparison executes sequentially, so the same layout buys nothing there and costs nothing either. Colliding entrypoint pairs: 0 of 15.

findings.title: How long before your app can say the transaction is done
findings.description: Monad reaches deterministic finality in 600 ms, two consensus slots. Base and Arbitrum One confirm through a single sequencer within a couple of seconds, but that confirmation is a promise from the operator; irreversible settlement waits on Ethereum, and a withdrawal waits seven days. Ethereum itself takes about 12.8 minutes. Which number matters depends on what the user is allowed to do next. Affects base, arbitrum. Monad hard finality: 600 ms.

findings.title: Rollups charge for calldata on top of execution gas
findings.description: Base, Arbitrum One publish every transaction's calldata to Ethereum and bill for it separately, and the figures here are execution gas only. The traced calls carry a median of 52 bytes each. Measured against those chains' own fee oracles the omitted charge is fractions of a cent even for a 39 KB deployment, since EIP-4844 blobs made data posting nearly free, so it is a real gap rather than a large one. It moves with Ethereum's fee market, not with your contract. Affects base, arbitrum. Median calldata: 52 B.

findings.title: Monad has no global mempool
findings.description: Transactions are forwarded to the next few block leaders rather than gossiped network-wide, so anything that watches pending transactions works differently. This contract does not appear to depend on pending-transaction visibility, so it is context rather than a change. Affects monad.

findings.fix: Either remove the dead require and rely on checked arithmetic, or check for overflow explicitly before adding so the custom message is emitted. Update the tests to match.
findings.title: add96 overflow check is dead code under Solidity 0.8; custom error message never emitted
findings.description:
Revert reasons for balance or vote overflow differ from the original 0.5/0.6 Compound contract. Off-chain tooling or tests that match the message text could break. Safety is unaffected, because the transaction still reverts.

What the attacker gets: Nothing is lost. The only effect is a changed revert reason that may confuse integrators.

What has to be true first: A destination balance or delegate vote total would exceed 2^96. This is unreachable in practice because the total supply is 1e25, well below 2^96 (about 7.9e28).

How it is exploited:
No exploit. An overflowing sum on line 286 reverts with a built-in arithmetic panic, because checked arithmetic is active in 0.8. The require on line 287 can therefore never fail, and the custom messages passed at lines 238 and 256 are never emitted.

findings.fix: Require a non-zero recipient in the constructor. Verify the recipient address in the deployment script. Have the recipient delegate right after deployment.
findings.title: Constructor sends full supply to an unvalidated address, which starts undelegated
findings.description:
A bad constructor argument permanently locks all 10M tokens. A correct recipient that never delegates leaves its voting weight unused.

What the attacker gets: The deployer loses the entire supply if the constructor argument is wrong. This is a deployment-time operational risk, not an exploitable defect.

What has to be true first: A deployment mistake. It is detectable immediately after deployment.

How it is exploited:
No attacker is needed. The deployer passes address(0) or a wrong address as the account argument. Line 64 credits the entire supply to it, and the contract has no mint or admin function to recover it. Even with the correct recipient, delegates[account] is zero, so the supply carries no votes until that account calls delegate.

chains.name: Monad
caveats: Gas is charged on the transaction's gas limit, not the gas it uses, so a padded limit is money spent.
Cold account access costs 10,100 gas against 2,600 elsewhere, which makes call-heavy contracts use more gas units.
There is no global mempool. Transactions are forwarded to the next few leaders instead.
EIP-4844 blob transactions are not supported.
Full nodes do not serve arbitrary historical state, so some indexing patterns need an archive provider.
EIP-7702 delegated accounts cannot be taken below 10 MON and cannot use CREATE or CREATE2.
The ecosystem is younger than the established L2s, so fewer battle-tested integrations exist.

chains.name: Ethereum
caveats: The most expensive execution environment of the group by a wide margin.
Two epochs, roughly 12.8 minutes, before a block is economically final.
24 KB contract size limit forces large systems into proxies or diamonds.

chains.name: Base
caveats: A single sequencer orders every transaction, so liveness depends on one operator.
Each transaction pays an L1 data fee on top of execution gas, which dominates for calldata-heavy calls.
Withdrawals to Ethereum sit behind a seven-day challenge window.
Execution is sequential, so a parallel-friendly contract layout buys nothing.

chains.name: Arbitrum One
caveats: `block.number` returns an L1 block number, which breaks contracts that assume L2 block cadence.
Transactions pay an L1 data component that is often larger than execution gas.
A single sequencer orders every transaction.
Withdrawals to Ethereum sit behind a seven-day challenge window.
Execution is sequential, so a parallel-friendly contract layout buys nothing.

chains.name: Polygon PoS
caveats: Security comes from its own validator set rather than from Ethereum.
Execution is sequential, so a parallel-friendly contract layout buys nothing.
Historically prone to reorgs of several blocks under load.

chains.name: BNB Smart Chain
caveats: A small validator set relative to Ethereum.
Execution is sequential, so a parallel-friendly contract layout buys nothing.

Gas figures come from executing the contract in a local EVM with synthesised arguments. A function guarded by a balance or permission check will revert, and reverted calls are marked rather than counted.
Only state-changing functions are traced. View and pure functions cost nothing to call from outside a transaction.

Only execution and intrinsic gas is modelled. Rollups additionally charge for publishing calldata to Ethereum, which is not included. Measured against the live oracles, that fee is around $0.0001 on Base and $0.00002 on Arbitrum even for a 39 KB deployment, three to four orders of magnitude below the execution cost shown, because EIP-4844 blobs made data posting nearly free.
Ethereum storage cost is measured from the EVM. The Monad figure is that measurement adjusted by the published MIP-8 schedule.

What the attacker gets: Nothing is lost. The only effect is a changed revert reason that may confuse integrators.

What has to be true first: A destination balance or delegate vote total would exceed 2^96. This is unreachable in practice because the total supply is 1e25, well below 2^96 (about 7.9e28).

How it is exploited:
No exploit. An overflowing sum on line 286 reverts with a built-in arithmetic panic, because checked arithmetic is active in 0.8. The require on line 287 can therefore never fail, and the custom messages passed at lines 238 and 256 are never emitted.
findings.fix: Either remove the dead require and rely on checked arithmetic, or check for overflow explicitly before adding so the custom message is emitted. Update the tests to match.

findings.title: Constructor sends full supply to an unvalidated address, which starts undelegated
findings.description:
A bad constructor argument permanently locks all 10M tokens. A correct recipient that never delegates leaves its voting weight unused.

What the attacker gets: The deployer loses the entire supply if the constructor argument is wrong. This is a deployment-time operational risk, not an exploitable defect.

What has to be true first: A deployment mistake. It is detectable immediately after deployment.

How it is exploited:
No attacker is needed. The deployer passes address(0) or a wrong address as the account argument. Line 64 credits the entire supply to it, and the contract has no mint or admin function to recover it. Even with the correct recipient, delegates[account] is zero, so the supply carries no votes until that account calls delegate.
findings.fix: Require a non-zero recipient in the constructor. Verify the recipient address in the deployment script. Have the recipient delegate right after deployment.

issues.title: Block Timestamp Dependency
issues.description: Block timestamps can be manipulated by miners within a short range
issues.recommendation: Avoid using timestamps for critical logic or accept ~15 second variance

chains.name: Monad
caveats: Gas is charged on the transaction's gas limit, not the gas it uses, so a padded limit is money spent.
Cold account access costs 10,100 gas against 2,600 elsewhere, which makes call-heavy contracts use more gas units.
There is no global mempool. Transactions are forwarded to the next few leaders instead.
EIP-4844 blob transactions are not supported.
Full nodes do not serve arbitrary historical state, so some indexing patterns need an archive provider.
EIP-7702 delegated accounts cannot be taken below 10 MON and cannot use CREATE or CREATE2.
The ecosystem is younger than the established L2s, so fewer battle-tested integrations exist.

chains.name: Ethereum
caveats: The most expensive execution environment of the group by a wide margin.
Two epochs, roughly 12.8 minutes, before a block is economically final.
24 KB contract size limit forces large systems into proxies or diamonds.

chains.name: Base
caveats: A single sequencer orders every transaction, so liveness depends on one operator.
Each transaction pays an L1 data fee on top of execution gas, which dominates for calldata-heavy calls.
Withdrawals to Ethereum sit behind a seven-day challenge window.
Execution is sequential, so a parallel-friendly contract layout buys nothing.

chains.name: Arbitrum One
caveats: `block.number` returns an L1 block number, which breaks contracts that assume L2 block cadence.
Transactions pay an L1 data component that is often larger than execution gas.
A single sequencer orders every transaction.
Withdrawals to Ethereum sit behind a seven-day challenge window.
Execution is sequential, so a parallel-friendly contract layout buys nothing.

chains.name: Polygon PoS
caveats: Security comes from its own validator set rather than from Ethereum.
Execution is sequential, so a parallel-friendly contract layout buys nothing.
Historically prone to reorgs of several blocks under load.

chains.name: BNB Smart Chain
caveats: A small validator set relative to Ethereum.
Execution is sequential, so a parallel-friendly contract layout buys nothing.

findings.title: Gas variance costs real money on Monad
findings.detail: Monad debits the sender for the transaction's gas limit, not the gas it uses, so anything a wallet pads onto the estimate is spent. solc cannot bound allowance(address,address), approve(address,uint256), delegate(address) and 7 more, which is where wallets fall back to a large default limit.
findings.action: Bound the loops, and have your frontend set an explicit gas limit for operations whose cost is fixed rather than letting the wallet estimate and pad.

findings.title: Storage is spread too thinly to amortise Monad's page charge
findings.detail: 4 slots across 4 pages. Monad pays 8,100 gas for the first touch of each 128-slot page, so slots that sit alone on a page cost more than they would on a per-slot schedule. Summed over the 3 calls traced, that is +23,700 gas.
findings.action: Group state that is read together into a struct so it lands on one page. Each mapping key gets its own page, but a struct stored under that key shares it.

findings.title: Contract is shaped for parallel execution
findings.detail: 5 of 5 entrypoints can run concurrently, grade B. 0 of 15 entrypoint pairs always collide, and 11 more collide when they touch the same key, on balances, checkpoints, delegates. This only converts into throughput on a chain that executes transactions in parallel. Monad does; every other chain in this comparison executes sequentially, so the same layout buys nothing there and costs nothing either.

findings.title: How long before your app can say the transaction is done
findings.detail: Monad reaches deterministic finality in 600 ms, two consensus slots. Base and Arbitrum One confirm through a single sequencer within a couple of seconds, but that confirmation is a promise from the operator; irreversible settlement waits on Ethereum, and a withdrawal waits seven days. Ethereum itself takes about 12.8 minutes. Which number matters depends on what the user is allowed to do next.

findings.title: Rollups charge for calldata on top of execution gas
findings.detail: Base, Arbitrum One publish every transaction's calldata to Ethereum and bill for it separately, and the figures here are execution gas only. The traced calls carry a median of 52 bytes each. Measured against those chains' own fee oracles the omitted charge is fractions of a cent even for a 39 KB deployment, since EIP-4844 blobs made data posting nearly free, so it is a real gap rather than a large one. It moves with Ethereum's fee market, not with your contract.

findings.title: Monad has no global mempool
findings.detail: Transactions are forwarded to the next few block leaders rather than gossiped network-wide, so anything that watches pending transactions works differently. This contract does not appear to depend on pending-transaction visibility, so it is context rather than a change.

caveats: Gas figures come from executing the contract in a local EVM with synthesised arguments. A function guarded by a balance or permission check will revert, and reverted calls are marked rather than counted.
Only state-changing functions are traced. View and pure functions cost nothing to call from outside a transaction.

Only execution and intrinsic gas is modelled. Rollups additionally charge for publishing calldata to Ethereum, which is not included. Measured against the live oracles, that fee is around $0.0001 on Base and $0.00002 on Arbitrum even for a 39 KB deployment, three to four orders of magnitude below the execution cost shown, because EIP-4844 blobs made data posting nearly free.
Ethereum storage cost is measured from the EVM. The Monad figure is that measurement adjusted by the published MIP-8 schedule.
